# The observable algebra generated by transporting one five-state grading

19 November 2026. Conditional hand proof. At 4d379d485 the geometric one-return quotient generated G=SL(2,F25). In its specified Weil representation on H=C^5 ⊗ C^5 the longitude is L=Pjoint D, where D|u,v>=ζ^(3uv)|u,v> and Pjoint flips both coordinates. A dimension bound for linear representations does not settle whether one coordinate can survive as a reduced open system. The following tests address that question directly.

## A partial trace does not close under the actual longitude

Take |+>=sum_u |u>/sqrt(5). All product inputs |+>⊗|v> have the same first-coordinate reduced state. After L the first-coordinate amplitudes are Fourier characters indexed by v up to sign. For v=0 and v=1 they are orthogonal. No input-independent channel on the first coordinate alone implements that evolution for all allowed joint states. Choosing a companion distribution or a persistent record of it is an additional state assumption. With a specified independent diagonal companion of probabilities p_v the reduced off-diagonal (u,u′) acquires factor sum_v p_v ζ^(3(u−u′)v), up to the final parity. A uniform companion erases these coherences, a sharp one preserves their magnitudes. Both are legitimate different preparations. The same conclusions hold with the two coordinates exchanged.

For an arbitrary first-coordinate operator, conjugating its matrix unit |u><u′|⊗I by D appends the companion phase diag_v ζ^(3(u−u′)v). The transformed observable stays on the first coordinate only if its off-diagonal matrix entries vanish. The prime-subfield Fourier element is a product of two Fourier transforms (possibly rescaled or inverted by convention). Requiring the same closure after that transform forces a diagonal observable to be diagonal in a Fourier basis too, hence scalar. Thus no nontrivial algebra confined to this coordinate is covariant under the whole returned geometric action.

## Minimal enlargement has an exact answer

Use unital complex adjoint-closed algebras of observables. Closure means invariance under conjugation by the image of every g in G. Let Pu be the first-coordinate parity. Its ± eigenspaces on a single C^5 give the 3+2 split used by B1951. Transporting this grading, or either of its spectral projectors, forces precisely the algebra

    End(H_joint-even) ⊕ End(H_joint-odd) = M_13(C) ⊕ M_12(C).

Indeed Pu commutes with Pjoint and takes D to D⁻¹. The generated algebra contains Pu(L Pu L⁻¹)=D⁻² and hence D since D has order five. This is the Weil image of the upper unipotent U(−2δ). By conjugation with the diagonal torus the algebra then contains images of all U(−2δ s²), s∈F25×. The nonzero squares, of which there are twelve, span F25 over F5 because any one-dimensional subspace has only four nonzero elements. Products and powers generate all U(z). Conjugating by the Weyl element supplies lower unipotents. The algebra thus contains the whole image of G and its linear span.

To check the span, use the symmetrically phased Heisenberg translations W(a,b), (a,b)∈k², k=F25. They are an orthogonal basis of End(H): different shifts have disjoint diagonals and different modulations on the same diagonal are orthogonal by additive-character summation. Weil conjugation permutes these operators by its symplectic action on k² without residual phases, using the symmetric ordering with the factor 1/2. This is the defining Heisenberg intertwining property of the finite Weil action; equivalently it follows on an elementary shear by expanding (x+a)² and on a Fourier generator by character summation. G has precisely two orbits, zero and all nonzero vectors (complete a nonzero vector to a determinant-one basis). Its commutant therefore has dimension two. I and Pjoint already commute with G and are independent. By the finite-dimensional double commutant theorem the span of the unitary group image is exactly the displayed joint block algebra. Finally Pu itself commutes with Pjoint, so adjoining it and its entire orbit cannot enlarge that algebra. Its complex dimension is 313. This establishes minimality in both directions.

If one starts with the *entire* first-coordinate matrix algebra, its conjugated shift by D gives a product of that shift and a nontrivial companion phase. Multiplying by the inverse shift produces the companion phase alone. A product Fourier transform supplies its companion shift. These generate the second-coordinate matrix algebra, hence the full M_25(C). This is a stronger initial demand than keeping only a parity reading. The two results should not be interchanged.

The derivation shows exactly what information must accompany a particular measurement if every geometric transport is admitted. It does not justify G as physical gauge group, specify a four-dimensional measuring interaction, select a history, derive a quantum state, or supply subjective awareness. A different instrument, another allowed register, or a dynamical restriction to fewer transformations has a different closure question. In particular a finite exterior Fock space on a separate five-sheet cover is a distinct construction.

For the finite-field-extension formulation and Heisenberg intertwining see Gurevich and Hadani, §§0.5.1 and 1.2, [primary paper](https://people.math.wisc.edu/~sgurevich/YACHA673.pdf). The matrix-size calculation is independent of any repository numerical tolerance. All scientific execution and non-authoring review remain separate.
